issues.issue: Section 1 fixes "Lender" as the party to this Agreement that lends the Securities, but Annex I-A (Party Acting as Agent) ¶5 deems references to "Lender" to mean the Agent's undisclosed Principal. Whether Wells Fargo or its lending Principals is the "Lender" for purposes of this Agreement cannot be settled from Section 1 alone.

A Confirmation becomes "conclusive evidence" of the Loan terms unless "specific objection is made promptly after receipt," and "promptly" is given no period or benchmark. The consequence of silence is total, so the length of the objection window is a live question.

Section 2.2 says no Loan occurs until both the Loaned Securities and the Collateral have been transferred, which cannot be squared with Section 4.1 (Collateral may follow the securities up to Close of Business) and Section 4.4 (which presupposes a one-sided transfer under an existing Loan). Whether a Loan exists during that interval is left open.

The delivery deadline is "the Cutoff Time," which Section 25.16 leaves to Schedule B or, failing agreement, to "market practice"; Schedule B fixes no such time. The transfer deadline in this section therefore has no ascertainable content on the face of the instrument.

Section 3.2 requires a schedule and receipt only "for each Loan in which Lender is a Customer," while Section 2.1 treats a schedule and receipt "in accordance with Section 3.2" as a general means of confirming any Loan. Whether the schedule-and-receipt route is available for non-Customer Loans is unresolved.

The security interest springs up if a Loan "is deemed to be a loan of money," without saying by whom, under what law, or at what time such a deeming occurs. The trigger for the fallback pledge is therefore indeterminate.

Section 4.1 lets Collateral arrive as late as Close of Business on the day the Loaned Securities are transferred, while Section 2.2 provides that no Loan occurs until the Collateral has been transferred. The two cannot both describe the same intervening period.

The same sentence permits Lender to "use or invest the Collateral, if such consists of cash, at its own risk" and then obliges a non-Broker-Dealer Lender to "segregate Collateral from all securities or other assets in its possession." Whether cash Collateral may be commingled and reinvested, and what "at its own risk" allocates, are both left in doubt by these words.

Read with Annex I-A ¶5, which deems "Lender" to mean the Agent's Principal, the phrase "at its own risk" places cash-collateral investment loss on the Principal rather than the investing Agent. That reading cannot be squared with Annex I-A ¶3's limitation of the Agent's liabilities as drafted.

Section 4.3 requires Lender to transfer back "the Collateral (as adjusted pursuant to Section 9)," but Section 25.11 defines Collateral to include the securities in which cash collateral has been "invested or reinvested" and their proceeds. Whether Lender must return the original cash amount or only the reinvestment assets at whatever value cannot be determined from the two read together.

The "absolute right to the return" of Collateral or Loaned Securities on a failed exchange sits against Section 2.2, under which no Loan has even arisen until both transfers occur, and against Section 4.2's lien attaching on transfer. Which regime governs the unmatched transfer is unclear.

The proviso listing permissible substitute Collateral breaks off after "(a) consist only of cash," so the categories of acceptable substitution cannot be read from the text. "Reasonable notice ... taking into account all relevant factors" likewise sets no measurable period.

Option (c) permits Borrower to transfer "such other Collateral to Lender as may be acceptable to Lender," giving Lender an unbounded veto with no standard of acceptability. Whether Lender must act reasonably in refusing substitute Collateral is unstated.

Both the Loan Fee and the Cash Collateral Fee are payable "at such rates as Borrower and Lender may agree," fixing no rate and no fallback if no rate is agreed. The pricing term is an agreement to agree.

For Government Securities, fees fall due "at such other times, if any, as may be customary in accordance with market practice," a payment date with no ascertainable content in the document. Which market's practice governs is not said.

Fees become payable "immediately in the event of a Default," yet Section 12.8 makes non-payment of fees a Default only after notice and a cure period running to the next day's Cutoff Time. The acceleration and the cure regime pull in opposite directions.

Section 6.1(b) lets Borrower terminate a cash-collateralized Loan on any Business Day, while Annex III makes all Loans of non-Equity Securities "Term Loans" and Annex III ¶5 charges a Breakage Fee to the party requesting early termination. Whether the 6.1(b) right is free-standing or conditioned by the Annex is unresolved.

Section 6.2 requires Lender to transfer the Collateral "upon such transfer by Borrower," but the cross-referenced Section 4.3 permits the return to slip to the next day on which a transfer may be effected under Section 15. The simultaneity this section promises is not what Section 4.3 delivers.

The carve-out reads "Except as set forth in Sections 3.1 and 8.2," but Section 3.1 concerns Lender's transfer of the Loaned Securities and has nothing to except from Borrower's incidents of ownership; the intended reference is evidently Section 8.1 (Lender's right to Distributions). The mis-citation changes what is excepted from Borrower's ownership rights.

Borrower's waiver of voting rights in Collateral operates only "if Lender may, pursuant to Section 4.2, Retransfer Collateral," and Section 4.2 permits Retransfer only if Lender is a Broker-Dealer or Borrower has defaulted. Whether a bank Lender's Collateral is caught by the waiver depends on a status question the section does not answer.

Lender's entitlement to all Distributions on Loaned Securities stands against Section 7.1, which gives Borrower "all of the incidents of ownership" including the right to transfer the securities to others. What Lender is owed when Borrower has on-lent or sold the securities is worked out only by reading the two together.

The sentence governing non-cash Distributions after a Loan has terminated breaks off at "Borrower shall forthwith transfer the ...," leaving the object and timing of that obligation unstated. The conditioning of payment on Lender "not [being] in Default" also has no stated consequence if the condition fails.

The gross-up is triggered by "any withholding or other tax, duty, fee, levy or charge required to be deducted or withheld," a catch-all whose outer edge against the enumerated fiscal charges is undefined. Whether non-tax deductions fall within "Tax" is open.
The limitation turns on a Payee having "failed timely to provide" a certificate or documentation, with no deadline stated anywhere for its provision. "Timely" has no benchmark in the Agreement.

The operative condition reads "transfer of cash cash or other property by Lender would give rise to a Margin Deficit," omitting the parallel Borrower branch that the following words ("Borrower or Lender (as the case may be)") presuppose. As written the crediting mechanism cannot be applied to a Borrower transfer.

Section 9.1 fixes a hard 100% daily collateralization test when Lender is a Customer, while Sections 9.2 and 25.37 measure margin by the "Margin Percentage," which Schedule B ¶6 restates at a different level. Which figure governs a Loan to a Customer Lender is not settled by this section.

Section 9.2 measures the Margin Deficit on the aggregate of all Loans, while Section 9.1 imposes a per-Loan 100% test and Section 9.4 allows loan-by-loan valuation only by agreement. Which basis controls absent an express agreement is left open.

The agreed threshold applies to "the respective rights of Lender and Borrower under Sections 9.2 and 9.3" but is silent on Section 9.1's mandatory daily 100% mark when Lender is a Customer. Whether a threshold can cut down the Section 9.1 duty is not addressed.

Everything turns on the "Margin Notice Deadline," which Section 25.36 leaves to the Confirmation, Schedule B or, failing that, "market practice"; no time is set in the executed Schedule B. The same-day/next-day divide therefore rests on an unfixed hour.

This no-reliance representation overlaps with, but is worded differently from, the further no-reliance representations added by Schedule B ¶5, which Schedule B ¶2 says governs in case of inconsistency. Which formulation measures a reliance claim is not resolved.

The representation is qualified by compliance with "Section 11.1(b)," which requires execution of and compliance with "Annex I," but Schedule B ¶1 makes "Annex I-A" the applicable agency annex. The chain of cross-references does not close on an existing document.

The permitted purposes are short sales and failures to receive, "or as otherwise permitted pursuant to Regulation T," a catch-all sitting against two enumerated specifics. How far the general words extend beyond the listed purposes is open.

The subsection makes "Lender" the party deemed to represent that it is an "exempted borrower" under Regulation T or a market maker financing its activities — a representation that on its face belongs to Borrower, and it also refers back to "subsection (6)" rather than subsection (a). As written the substituted representation is given by the wrong party.

Section 11.2 lets Borrower satisfy financial-disclosure demands with its "most recent publicly-available financial statements," while Section 17.4(b) requires audited and unaudited statements of Borrower's financial condition before any Loan is made. The two disclosure standards are not reconciled.

Lender's remedies must be exercised "in a commercially reasonable manner," a standard the Agreement nowhere defines, and the same section lets Lender elect a deemed purchase at a price "obtained from a generally recognized source" in its sole discretion. What makes the repurchase or sale commercially reasonable is precisely what a defaulting Borrower would contest.

Borrower may elect "in its sole discretion" to be deemed to have bought Replacement Collateral or sold the Loaned Securities at a price "obtained from a generally recognized source or the last bid quotation," with no requirement that the chosen source be reasonable. The deemed-price mechanism and the commercial-reasonableness standard in the same section pull apart.

Section 13.3(b) lets the non-defaulting party establish the pricing source "in its sole discretion," which cannot be squared with Sections 13.1 and 13.2 requiring purchases and sales to be made "in a commercially reasonable manner." Whether the valuation is reviewable for reasonableness turns on which controls.

Preserving "any rights otherwise available ... under any other agreement or applicable law" sits against the detailed and apparently exhaustive liquidation formulae of Sections 13.1 and 13.2. Whether the contractual measure of damages is exclusive is left open by this saving clause.

A transfer day is excluded if "the transferee is closed for business at its address set forth in Schedule A," but Schedule A lists several addresses in different states for each party without designating one for this purpose. Which office's closure blocks a transfer is not determinable.

The section defines "securities" to include security entitlements "except in this Section 15," so the one Section governing transfers of securities uses the term in a sense different from the rest of the Agreement. The clause listing the transferor's steps also breaks off mid-sentence at "(within the meaning of."

Lender must give the Plan-assets notice "upon the execution of this Agreement or upon initiation of such Loan under Section 2.1," without saying which occasion controls or what follows if neither notice is given. The trigger for conducting a Loan under PTE 81-6 is therefore uncertain.

The representation flips to Lender if Lender "fails to communicate and keep current" Plan information, with no standard for currency, no deadline, and no materiality qualifier. When the shift occurs is left to argument.

Section 17.3 requires daily marking "pursuant to Section 9.7," and there is no Section 9.7 in the Agreement — Section 9 ends at 9.6, and the Customer mark-to-market rule is Section 9.1. The obligation points to a provision that does not exist.

Section 17.4(c) lets Lender terminate "at any time" with delivery within a period measured from the customary delivery cycle or five Business Days, which cannot be squared with Section 6.1(a)'s termination-date regime keyed to the standard settlement date on notice. Which timetable governs a PTE 81-6 Loan is unresolved.

Section 18 makes all Loans a single agreement with cross-default and cross-Loan setoff, while Annex I-A ¶4 provides that the portion of each Loan allocable to each Principal is a separate agreement with that Principal. Cross-Loan netting against a multi-principal Agent cannot be given effect under both.

This Agreement is governed by New York law, while the Securities Lending Agreement under which Wells Fargo lends the same securities as agent is governed by Minnesota law. Which law governs the collateral and risk-of-loss questions arising from a single lending transaction is not settled by either clause.

The last sentence requires a writing only for "waivers in respect of a Default," leaving waivers of every other term to be established without a writing despite the opening non-waiver sentence. The two sentences set different rules for different waivers with no stated boundary.

Section 21 makes all remedies and obligations survive termination of the Agreement, while Section 24.1 says termination is "subject only to fulfillment of any obligations then outstanding." What survives a notice of termination cannot be read from either alone.

A notice is "deemed effective" when received or, if not received, when "delivery was in good faith attempted," so an undelivered demand can start margin and cure clocks. "Good faith attempted" is given no evidentiary content.

Jurisdiction is submitted to "SOLELY FOR THE PURPOSE OF" enforcement proceedings, yet the same sentence extends to any proceeding "RELATING IN ANY WAY TO THIS AGREEMENT." The limiting word and the expansive words describe different scopes.

The supersession clause is itself subject to whatever "the parties" may otherwise agree, with no requirement of writing, while the later sentence of Section 24.1 permits modification only by a signed writing. Whether an unwritten side understanding survives supersession is unresolved.

The bar on assignment without consent does not say whether an Agent's substitution or reallocation of Principals under Annex I-A is an assignment of the Agreement. Annex I-A contemplates changes of Principal without Borrower's consent to the Agreement itself.

Termination on notice is "subject only to fulfillment of any obligations then outstanding," which cannot be squared with Section 21's provision that all remedies and Loan obligations survive termination of the Agreement. The two describe different post-termination positions.

Modification is permitted only by a signed writing, yet Section 24.2 expressly allows agreements under Sections 10.5(b) and 25.37 to be made orally, and dozens of operative provisions apply only "unless otherwise agreed" without requiring a writing. Whether an oral variation of a Loan term is effective turns on which sentence prevails.

"Time is of the essence" for each Loan cannot be squared with Sections 12.4 and 12.8, which make a failure to transfer or pay a Default only after notice and a cure period running to the next day's Cutoff Time. Whether a late transfer is instantly actionable is left in doubt.

Treating "each provision and agreement herein ... as separate and independent from any other provision" sits against Section 18, by which all Loans constitute a single agreement entered into in consideration of one another. The severability sentence, read literally, would undo the single-agreement premise.

The sentence opens "Any 4 between Borrower and Lender pursuant to Section 10.5(b) or Section 25.37," omitting the noun (agreement) that the formal requirements attach to. What class of dealings must satisfy clauses (a)–(c) cannot be read from the words.

An Act of Insolvency includes the appointment of an official for "any substantial part of its property," with no measure of substantiality. Since the consequence is automatic termination of all Loans, the boundary of the term matters.

The definition sweeps in any broker or dealer "regardless of whether the activities of such person are conducted in the United States or otherwise require such person to register," so a bank with dealer-type activities may qualify. Because Section 4.2 excuses a Broker-Dealer Lender from segregating Collateral and lets it Retransfer, the breadth of this definition decides those duties.

A Business Day is a day on which regular trading occurs "in the principal market" for the relevant Securities, a market the Agreement never identifies for any Loan. Deadlines throughout Sections 6, 9 and 12 depend on that unidentified market.

The definition assigns "Cash Collateral Fee" the meaning given in "Section 3.1," but Section 3.1 concerns the transfer of Loaned Securities; the term is defined in Section 5.1. The cross-reference points to the wrong provision.

"Close of Business" is whatever the parties agree in Schedule B "or otherwise orally or in writing" and, failing that, is "determined in accordance with market practice"; the executed Schedule B fixes no time. A deadline used throughout Sections 4, 6, 9 and 12 is left to unwritten practice.

"Collateral" is defined to include the accounts in which cash collateral is deposited, the securities in which it is "invested or reinvested," and the proceeds of both, yet Sections 4.3 and 6.2 simply require "the Collateral" to be returned on termination. Whether Borrower is owed its cash back or only the reinvestment assets at their then value is the product of reading the definition against those return obligations.

"Customer" is defined by reference to Rule 15c3-3 status "to the extent that Borrower is subject to such Rule," so whether a given Lender is a Customer depends on an unstated regulatory characterization. Sections 3.2, 9.1 and 25.11 all switch on that status.

"Cutoff Time" is left to agreement "in Schedule B or otherwise orally or in writing" and, in the absence of agreement, to "market practice," and Schedule B fixes no such time. Every delivery deadline in Sections 3, 4, 6 and 12 rests on this undetermined hour.

"Distribution" is defined as any distribution "including, but not limited to" six enumerated categories, leaving the general words to be measured against the specifics. Whether items such as merger consideration or corporate-action proceeds are Distributions or instead substituted Loaned Securities under Section 25.33 is left open.

"Equity Security" is defined negatively as any security other than a "nonequity security" as defined in Regulation T, so its content depends entirely on a regulation "as in effect from time to time." Whether a given instrument is an Equity Security — which decides the Annex III Term Loan default rule — cannot be read from the Agreement.

The rate is the published rate "on that day," but the definition never says which day is meant — the date of purchase, of sale, or each day of accrual. Sections 13.1 and 13.2 apply the rate "as such rate fluctuates from day to day," leaving the reference ambiguous.

"Foreign Securities" are those "principally cleared and settled outside the United States," with no test for what makes clearing and settlement principal. The default interest rate under Sections 13.1–13.2 and the settlement date under Schedule B ¶3 both turn on this word.

The LIBOR definition breaks off at "(or, if at least two such rates appear, the arithmetic mean of," so the rate cannot be computed from the text where more than one quotation appears. The default interest rate in Sections 13.1 and 13.2 depends on this incomplete definition.
The definition of "Loan" ends at "shall have the meaning assigned in Section," with no section number given. The Agreement's central defined term points nowhere on its face.

The "Margin Notice Deadline" is left to the Confirmation, Schedule B or "market practice," and no such time appears in the executed Schedule B. Whether a margin call must be met the same day under Section 9.6 turns on an hour the documents never fix.

Section 25.37 fixes a Margin Percentage of not less than 100% subject to agreement under Section 24.2, while Schedule B ¶6 restates "Margin Percentage" on different terms and Schedule B ¶2 provides that the Schedule governs any inconsistency. Which percentage applies to a given Loan cannot be answered from Section 25.37 alone.

The definition ends by providing that the Market Value determinations "shall apply for all purposes under this Agreement, except for purposes of Section 13," while Section 13 itself supplies only a "generally recognized source" or last bid quotation chosen in the non-defaulting party's sole discretion. The valuation standard on default is thus carved out of the defined term without a substitute of equal content.

"Retransfer" lists pledging, lending, selling "or otherwise transfer[ring]" the Collateral, a catch-all sitting against the enumerated dealings. Whether investing or commingling cash Collateral under Section 4.2 is a "Retransfer" is left to the general words.

"Securities" is defined as "securities or, if agreed by the parties in writing, other assets" — a definition that defines the term by itself and then extends it to unspecified assets. The class of property that may be lent is therefore not fixed by the definition.

The securities-contract characterization is qualified "except insofar as the type of assets subject to the Loan would render such definition inapplicable," without saying who decides or by what test. Since Section 25.44 permits "other assets" to be lent, the exception may swallow the statement.

Every transfer is stated to be "a 'settlement payment' or a 'margin payment'" without saying which, though the two carry different statutory consequences. The disjunctive leaves the characterization of any particular transfer unresolved.

The FDIA provision runs into illegible and garbled text after "'securities contract' and 'qualified financial,'" so the conditions and consequences of insured-depository-institution status cannot be read from the instrument. Whether Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.'s status triggers these terms is unascertainable on the face of the document.

Section 26.5 (FDICIA treatment) is wholly garbled, with the definitions of "netting contract" and "covered contractual payment obligation" unreadable. The provision as executed cannot be given a determinate meaning.

Section 26.6 (master netting treatment) is likewise garbled, leaving the reference to "master netting agreement" status and to exchange or clearing organization rules unreadable. Its operative content cannot be determined from the text.

The SIPA disclosure states that the collateral delivered to Lender may constitute the only source of satisfaction of Borrower's obligation if Borrower fails to return the Loaned Securities, which cannot be squared with Section 13.1's provision that Borrower remains liable for any excess of the Replacement Securities' price over the Collateral. Whether Lender's recourse is limited to the Collateral is left contradicted.

The government-securities acknowledgment is largely illegible, so the scope of Lender's acknowledgment about the treatment of securities pledged by Borrower as Collateral cannot be read. What Lender is taken to have acknowledged is indeterminate.

The Annex describes itself as governing transactions in which "a party lending Securities ('Agent') ... is acting as agent," yet ¶1 speaks of the Principal performing "the obligations of Lender or Borrower, as the case may be." Whether the Annex reaches an agent acting for a borrowing Principal is left unclear.

Agent must supply "such information in its possession necessary to complete all required fields in the format generally used in the industry" and "use its best efforts" for optional information, neither standard being defined. What information is required and what effort suffices are both left at large.

If Agent fails to identify or allocate to an Approved Principal, Borrower may "terminate any Loan with such Principal or Principals" — a remedy exercisable against a Principal whose identity is by hypothesis undisclosed. The remedy also cuts across Section 6.1's notice-and-settlement-date termination mechanics.

The limitation of Agent's liabilities — that Agent shall not be treated or liable as principal unless expressly agreed — cannot be squared with Section 11.1, which requires each party either to be liable as principal or to execute and comply with the agency Annex. Whether Wells Fargo answers as principal on these Loans is the very point the two provisions divide on.

Annex I-A ¶4 deems the portion of each Loan allocable to a Principal a separate agreement with that Principal, which cannot stand with Section 18's single-agreement, cross-default and cross-Loan setoff regime. Which characterization governs a default by one Principal is left unresolved.

The interpretation paragraph deems references to "Lender" (and to "party" and "other party") to mean the Agent's Principal, contradicting Section 1 and Section 25.28, which define Lender as the contracting party that lends the Securities. Whose rights and risks Sections 4.2, 8 and 13 attach to depends on which reading prevails.

Annex II ¶1, the primary Market Value rule for exchange-quoted Securities, is garbled to the point that the applicable quotation, exchange and time cannot be read. Section 25.38 makes this Annex the governing definition of Market Value for every margin and remedy calculation.

Annex II ¶2, dealing with Securities quoted otherwise than on an exchange, is illegible in its operative terms, so the alternative quotation source and time cannot be determined. The fallback valuation rule has no readable content.

Annex II ¶3's market-practice valuation rule is garbled, leaving the trigger ("except as provided in Section ...") and the source of the quotation unreadable. What governs when no recognized quotation exists cannot be established from the text.
Annex II ¶4's rule for Foreign Securities is garbled, so it cannot be told which Close of Trading or which market determines value. Valuation of Foreign Securities collateral is left indeterminate.

Annex II ¶5, adjusting Market Value for accrued interest and for amounts credited under Section 8, is largely illegible. Whether accrued interest already transferred is added back cannot be read from the provision.

Annex II ¶6 applies its Market Value determinations for all purposes of the Agreement "except for purposes of Section 13," which leaves the default liquidation in Section 13 to be valued by a different and less specified standard. The carve-out cannot be reconciled with Section 13's own price mechanics.

The Annex defines Term Loans as loans made "against a pledge of cash Collateral," yet Annex III ¶1 makes every Loan of non-Equity Securities a Term Loan whatever the Collateral. The definition and the designation rule describe different populations of Loans.

The default rule that "[a]ll Loans of Securities other than Equity Securities shall be 'Term Loans' subject to this Annex" cannot be squared with Section 6.1, under which either party may terminate any Loan on notice without charge. Under the Annex the same termination triggers replacement-loan and Breakage Fee obligations.

On early termination the parties must "use their best efforts to negotiate in good faith" a Replacement Loan of "comparable or other Securities" — an agreement to agree with no fallback if negotiation fails except the Breakage Fee. What effort discharges the obligation, and what makes Securities comparable, are both undefined.

Annex III ¶4 lets Lender keep the Terminated Loan's Collateral as Collateral for the Replacement Loan, while Section 4.3 obliges Lender to return the Collateral on the day the Loan is terminated. Whether Borrower's return right survives the roll into a Replacement Loan is unresolved.

Annex III ¶5 charges the "party requesting termination" a Breakage Fee, which cannot be squared with Section 6.1's unqualified right of either party to terminate a Loan on notice. It also conditions the return of Collateral on no Default having occurred with respect to Borrower, unlike Section 4.3.

The definition and computation of the "Breakage Fee" — the entire measure of damages for a failed Replacement Loan under Annex III ¶5 — is garbled and unreadable in the executed document. The amount payable on early termination of a Term Loan cannot be computed from the text.

Schedule B names the contracting lender as "Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.," while the Securities Lending Agreement appointing the lending agent for the participant's account names Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, N.A. Which Wells Fargo entity is the "Lender" bound by this Agreement is not established by the recital.

Schedule B ¶1 makes "Annex I-A (Agency Annex)" part of the Agreement, but Section 11.1(b) requires a party acting other than as principal to "execute and comply fully with the provisions of Annex I." There is no Annex I, so the covenant and the list of applicable annexes do not match.

Schedule B ¶2 resolves inconsistency only "between the terms of the Agreement and this Schedule," saying nothing about conflicts with the Annexes that ¶1 makes part of the Agreement, or about the Confirmation hierarchy in Section 2.1. The order of precedence among Agreement, Annexes, Confirmation and Schedule is left incomplete.

The provision states that the standard settlement date for Foreign Securities "shall be the standard settlement date that would apply to a purchase or sale of such Foreign Securities ... in the principal market," defining the term by itself. It also leaves "the principal market" for Foreign Securities unidentified.

The parties are bound to "any uniform practices applicable to securities loans among members of" two trade associations, "as currently in effect, or successor provisions thereto," without identifying the documents or their content. What the Uniform Practices require — and when a successor provision changes them — is not ascertainable from the instrument.

The added no-reliance representations are garbled beyond legibility after the introductory sentence, so what each party is representing about its own evaluation of each Loan cannot be read. The representations also overlap with, without matching, Section 10.2.

Schedule B ¶6 restates the "Margin Percentage" definition in terms that conflict with Section 25.37's "not less than 100%," and Schedule B ¶2 makes the Schedule govern; the restated percentages are moreover garbled in the executed copy. What margin level Borrower must maintain cannot be settled without construing the two definitions together.
